a. Why is the formation of cleavage furrow not possible in the cytokinesis of a plant cell?  (1 Mark)

b. Describe how cytokinesis takes place in a plant cell.  (2 Marks)

a. Formation of a cleavage furrow is not possible in plant cells because they are enclosed by a rigid, inextensible cellulose cell wall that prevents the plasma membrane from pinching inward from the outside.

b. In plant cells, cytokinesis takes place via cell plate (phragmoplast) formation:
1. Vesicles derived from the Golgi apparatus gather and align at the equatorial plane during telophase.
2. These Golgi vesicles fuse from the centre outward (centrifugally) to form a membrane-bound disc called the cell plate / phragmoplast.
3. The cell plate expands until its membranes fuse with the parental plasma membrane, and pectins and cellulose are deposited to form the middle lamella and new primary cell walls, dividing the parent cell into two daughter cells.

a. 1 mark for stating that the rigid cellulose cell wall prevents the plasma membrane from furrowing/pinching inward.
b. 1 mark for describing the alignment and fusion of Golgi vesicles at the equator to form the phragmoplast / cell plate; 1 mark for describing the outward fusion of the cell plate with the plasma membrane and deposition of the new cell wall.

a. Pancreas acts both as endocrine and exocrine gland.

With reference to the endocrine nature of pancreas, mention
i. the names of hormones it produces.  (2 Marks)
ii. any ONE way in which each of these hormones maintain the blood glucose concentration.  (2 Marks)
iii. any ONE effect of hypo-secretion of each hormone on the body.  (2 Marks)

i. Two hormones produced by the endocrine pancreas (islets of Langerhans):
1. Insulin (secreted by beta cells)
2. Glucagon (secreted by alpha cells)

ii. Maintenance of blood glucose concentration:
• Insulin lowers elevated blood glucose by stimulating cells throughout the body to take up glucose and directing the liver and skeletal muscle to convert glucose into stored glycogen (glycogenesis).
• Glucagon raises depressed blood glucose by stimulating hepatocytes in the liver to break down glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis) and promoting gluconeogenesis.

iii. Effects of hypo-secretion:
• Hypo-secretion of insulin leads to diabetes mellitus (hyperglycaemia), characterized by persistent high blood sugar, glucose in urine (glycosuria), excessive urination (polyuria), excessive thirst (polydipsia), and fatigue.
• Hypo-secretion of glucagon leads to hypoglycaemia (abnormally low blood glucose), resulting in weakness, shakiness, dizziness, sweating, and confusion.

1 mark for naming insulin; 1 mark for naming glucagon.
1 mark for describing insulin's role in lowering blood glucose (cellular glucose uptake/glycogenesis); 1 mark for describing glucagon's role in raising blood glucose (glycogenolysis in liver).
1 mark for effect of insulin hypo-secretion (diabetes mellitus / hyperglycaemia); 1 mark for effect of glucagon hypo-secretion (hypoglycaemia / abnormally low blood sugar).

b. Explain the process of vegetative propagation in onion and ginger.  (6 Marks)

Vegetative propagation in onion and ginger occurs via specialized underground modified stems:

1. Vegetative propagation in Onion (by Bulb):
• An onion bulb is a highly condensed underground vertical shoot with a flattened basal stem disc.
• Thick, fleshy scale leaves encircle the stem disc and store reserves of food, sugars, and water.
• Clusters of fibrous adventitious roots emerge downward from the base of the stem disc to anchor the plant and absorb moisture.
• A central apical terminal bud (and axillary buds) develops into an aerial green photosynthetic shoot, which matures into an independent plant.

2. Vegetative propagation in Ginger (by Rhizome):
• Ginger propagates through a rhizome, which is an elongated, fleshy, horizontally growing underground stem.
• The rhizome displays distinct morphological nodes and internodes, shielded by dry, brown scale leaves.
• Vegetative buds located at the nodes sprout upward during the growing season to form leafy aerial shoots, while adventitious roots grow downward from the lower surface into the soil.
• Branching rhizomes can fragment, and each piece bearing at least one viable node with a bud grows into a complete new ginger plant.

1 mark each for any 3 valid points describing onion propagation: propagation through bulb/condensed underground stem, presence of thick fleshy food-storing scale leaves, adventitious roots growing from the base, apical/axillary bud producing an aerial shoot.
1 mark each for any 3 valid points describing ginger propagation: propagation through rhizome/horizontal underground stem, presence of nodes and internodes with scale leaves, buds at nodes developing into aerial shoots and adventitious roots.

a. Describe how the following factors facilitate the process of evolution via natural selection.
i. Genetic variation  (4 Marks)
ii. Hereditary traits  (2 Marks)

i. Genetic variation facilitates natural selection (4 Marks):
1. Origin of variation: Heritable genetic differences arise within a population through random gene mutations, crossing over during meiosis, and independent assortment of chromosomes during sexual reproduction.
2. Phenotypic diversity: Genetic variation generates a diverse spectrum of physical, physiological, and behavioural traits among individuals in the population.
3. Differential adaptation: In a changing or challenging environment with limited resources, certain variations confer an adaptive advantage (such as superior camouflage, disease resistance, or foraging efficiency).
4. Differential survival and reproductive fitness: Individuals with advantageous variations are better fitted to survive environmental pressures (survival of the fittest) and reproduce more successfully than less-adapted peers.

ii. Hereditary traits facilitate natural selection (2 Marks):
1. Transmission to offspring: Because adaptive traits are encoded in DNA, surviving individuals pass their advantageous alleles directly to their offspring.
2. Evolutionary change in gene pool: Across successive generations, the frequency of beneficial adaptive alleles increases in the population while harmful alleles diminish, driving gradual evolution and adaptation of the species.

1 mark each for any 4 valid descriptive points for genetic variation: origin via mutation/meiosis, resulting in phenotypic diversity, providing differential adaptation to environmental challenges, enabling differential survival and reproductive fitness.
1 mark each for 2 points describing hereditary traits: passing advantageous alleles to offspring, increasing the proportion of adaptive traits in the population over generations leading to evolutionary change.

b. Describe how the following factors limit the population growth of an area.
i. Competition  (2 Marks)
ii. Predation  (2 Marks)
iii. Parasitism  (2 Marks)

Factors limiting population growth in an area:

i. Competition (2 Marks):
• When population density rises, individuals of the same species (intraspecific) or different species (interspecific) compete for limited essential resources such as food, water, nesting sites, sunlight, and mates.
• Resource limitation reduces individual nutrition, slows growth and reproduction, increases mortality among weaker competitors, and stabilizes the population at the environmental carrying capacity.

ii. Predation (2 Marks):
• Predators capture, kill, and consume prey organisms, directly removing individuals from the prey population and lowering their numbers.
• Increased predation prevents prey species from overpopulating their habitat, while predator and prey population sizes cycle dynamically to maintain ecological equilibrium.

iii. Parasitism (2 Marks):
• Parasites live on (ectoparasites) or inside (endoparasites) a host organism, deriving nutrients and energy at the host's expense.
• Heavy parasite loads weaken host health, stunt development, impair reproductive capacity, and transmit fatal pathogens, elevating mortality rates and curbing population growth.

2 marks for competition: 1 mark for describing competition for limited resources (food, water, territory); 1 mark for explaining that weaker competitors experience reduced survival and reproduction, capping population growth.
2 marks for predation: 1 mark for describing predators killing and consuming prey to directly lower numbers; 1 mark for regulating prey density within the environmental carrying capacity.
2 marks for parasitism: 1 mark for describing parasites draining host vitality and resources; 1 mark for explaining that weakened health, reduced fecundity, and disease transmission increase mortality and limit population size.
